title: Designing API Contracts
description: Learn to design clear, versioned API contracts that define the interface between system components and external clients.

data.text: An API contract is the formal agreement between a service and its consumers. It specifies endpoints, request formats, response formats, error codes, and authentication requirements. In system design interviews, discussing API contracts early signals that you think about interface design, backward compatibility, and client experience.

REST APIs use HTTP methods and resource-oriented URLs. A well-designed REST contract follows consistent naming, uses standard status codes, and returns predictable response shapes. Versioning is critical because changing an existing contract breaks all existing clients. Common versioning strategies include URL prefixes like /v1/ and media type versioning.

data.title: REST Contract Example — Create Order
data.content: API contract for creating an order in an e-commerce system

data.text: GraphQL uses a schema-first approach where the contract is defined in a schema definition language. The schema acts as both documentation and runtime validation. Clients request exactly the fields they need, reducing over-fetching and under-fetching. However, GraphQL contracts require careful field-level deprecation strategies.

data.title: Contract-First Design
data.text: Define the API contract before writing implementation code. In interviews, sketch the endpoints and data shapes on the whiteboard before discussing backend logic.

data.caption: API contract lifecycle
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Design Contract] --> B[Review with Stakeholders]
    B --> C[Implement Server]
    C --> D[Generate Client SDK]
    D --> E[Deploy v1]
    E --> F[Monitor Usage]
    F --> G{Breaking Change?}
    G -->|No| H[Patch / Minor Update]
    G -->|Yes| I[Version v2]
    H --> F
    I --> F

data.text: A complete API contract documents error responses. Standard HTTP status codes are not enough — your contract should specify the error schema, common error codes, and retry guidance. For example, a 429 Too Many Requests response should include a Retry-After header and a structured error body with the rate limit window.

terms.definition: A formal specification of an API's endpoints, request/response formats, and error handling.
The property that newer versions of an API do not break existing clients using older versions.
The process of updating an API contract over time while maintaining compatibility for existing consumers.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: API contracts define the interface between components
Versioning is mandatory for evolving systems
Error responses are part of the contract
data.takeaway: A well-defined API contract is the boundary that allows teams to work in parallel without stepping on each other's changes.
